ego.name: Lina Bo Bardi
ego.summary: Italian-born Brazilian modernist architect and designer who developed an influential practice in Brazil spanning architecture, exhibition design, publishing, and teaching; known for linking modernism to vernacular culture and public life (e.g., MASP and SESC Pompéia).

connections.relationship_description: Father; her early decision to become an architect met with limited support from him, but his adventurous, anarchist life is cited as an influence on her graphic representational style.
shared_activities: family life in Rome
early exposure to art and drawing influences
connections.notes: The article notes her father was not fully supportive of her architectural ambitions; it also attributes aspects of her drawing style to inspiration from him.

connections.relationship_description: Mother; part of her family background in Rome (parents of Achillina Bo, later Lina Bo Bardi).
shared_activities: family life in Rome
connections.notes: Less detailed in the article than her father, but explicitly named as her mother.

connections.relationship_description: Younger sister; mentioned as the second daughter of Enrico and Giovanna Bo.
shared_activities: childhood family life
connections.notes: The Wikipedia text provides minimal additional detail beyond identification.

connections.relationship_description: Early Milan collaborator; she worked with him at Studio Bo e Pagani and later traveled through postwar Italy with him for Domus commissions and co-founded a weekly architecture/culture magazine with him and Bruno Zevi.
shared_activities: work at Studio Bo e Pagani (Milan)
Domus-commissioned travel documenting postwar Italy (1945)
founding the weekly magazine A – Attualità, Architettura, Abitazione, Arte
connections.notes: One of her most documented early professional relationships.

connections.relationship_description: Architect/designer and editor; she collaborated with him on the magazine Lo Stile (until 1943) and later worked as Deputy Director of Domus (a magazine he founded).
shared_activities: magazine work on Lo Stile
professional network around Italian design publishing
connections.notes: The relationship is primarily professional/publishing and likely formative early in her career.

connections.relationship_description: Italian architect and critic; co-established with Bo Bardi and Carlo Pagani the weekly magazine A – Attualità, Architettura, Abitazione, Arte (A Cultura della Vita) in Milan.
shared_activities: founding/editing the weekly magazine A – Attualità, Architettura, Abitazione, Arte
connections.notes: Connects Bo Bardi to a broader postwar architectural debate and publishing network.

connections.relationship_description: Photographer who traveled with Bo Bardi and Carlo Pagani around Italy in 1945 for a Domus assignment documenting war damage and living conditions.
shared_activities: field documentation travel for Domus in postwar Italy
connections.notes: Short but well-defined collaboration tied to a specific reportage project.

connections.relationship_description: Writer/editor who directed the newspaper Milano Sera, where Bo Bardi collaborated as a contributor in the immediate postwar period.
shared_activities: journalistic collaboration with Milano Sera
connections.notes: Primarily an editorial/professional relationship via publication work.

connections.relationship_description: Husband and major lifelong collaborator; co-founded the magazine Habitat with her, and worked closely with her on MASP’s early organization and exhibition approaches.
shared_activities: marriage and relocation to Brazil (1946)
co-founding Habitat magazine
founding and developing MASP (São Paulo Museum of Art)
museum exhibition and spatial concepts (open exhibition space / innovative display)
connections.notes: Their partnership is presented as both personal and institutional (museum and publishing).

connections.relationship_description: Brazilian media magnate and arts patron; invited Pietro Maria Bardi to establish MASP and thereby became a key institutional sponsor enabling Bo Bardi’s museum work in São Paulo.
shared_activities: founding support for MASP
institutional patronage via Diários Associados
connections.notes: More of an enabling/patron relationship than a day-to-day collaboration.

connections.relationship_description: American architect; her early MASP sketches referenced the facade of the 1939 MoMA building designed by Goodwin (with Edward Durell Stone), indicating design influence on circulation and museum conception.
shared_activities: conceptual reference point for MASP early sketches (MoMA 1939 building)
connections.notes: Influence-based tie; no direct personal interaction is stated.

connections.relationship_description: American architect; co-designer (with Philip L. Goodwin) of MoMA’s 1939 building, cited indirectly as a reference in Bo Bardi’s early MASP sketches.
shared_activities: conceptual reference point for museum facade/circulation ideas (MoMA 1939 building)
connections.notes: Included as part of a specifically documented reference in the MASP founding narrative.

connections.relationship_description: Italian immigrant architect; collaborated with Bo Bardi on redesigning MASP exhibition spaces in the Diários Associados building (1950) and worked with her in the Studio d’Arte Palma (until 1951).
shared_activities: Studio d’Arte Palma (São Paulo)
redesign of MASP interiors/exhibition space (1950)
connections.notes: A central collaborator in her early Brazilian museum/interiors work.

connections.relationship_description: Member of the Studio d’Arte Palma team; responsible for the antiquarian section within the collective that included Bo Bardi, Pietro Maria Bardi, and Giancarlo Palanti.
shared_activities: Studio d’Arte Palma (shared studio and programmatic division of labor)
connections.notes: Included to represent the studio’s internal professional network and gender balance where documented.

connections.relationship_description: Polish architect whose building housed Studio d’Arte Palma (18th floor); Bo Bardi’s studio collective was located in a building by him.
shared_activities: shared physical/institutional context: Studio d’Arte Palma located in Korngold-designed building
connections.notes: Connection is primarily spatial/institutional (building author), not a documented close collaboration.

connections.relationship_description: Avant-garde artist/designer; Bo Bardi’s MASP exhibition redesign is described as influenced by interwar avant-garde practices including Lissitzky’s work.
shared_activities: exhibition design reference (interwar avant-garde display strategies)
connections.notes: Included because the Wikipedia text explicitly names these influences in relation to her exhibition design shift.

connections.relationship_description: Italian architect/designer; cited as an influence on Bo Bardi’s 1950 MASP exhibition approach within a lineage of interwar/modern display practices.
shared_activities: museum and exhibition design reference (modern display strategies)
connections.notes: The influence is framed through her exhibition design rethinking rather than direct personal contact.

connections.relationship_description: Modern architect; her Glass House is described as drawing from (among other works) Mies’s Farnsworth House, indicating a strong formal and conceptual influence.
shared_activities: architectural reference for the Glass House (Farnsworth House as precedent)
connections.notes: Influence tie grounded in explicit textual reference to a specific work.

connections.relationship_description: Designer/architect; her Glass House is described as drawing from American modernist works including Case Study House No. 8, associated with Charles Eames.
shared_activities: architectural precedent for domestic modernism (Case Study House No. 8 referenced)
connections.notes: Influence relationship; the Wikipedia text frames these as widely publicized references.

connections.relationship_description: Designer/architect; cited alongside Charles Eames via Case Study House No. 8 as an American modernist precedent referenced in discussion of Bo Bardi’s Glass House.
shared_activities: architectural precedent for domestic modernism (Case Study House No. 8 referenced)
connections.notes: Included separately from Charles Eames to represent the creative partnership while keeping each person unique in the network.

connections.relationship_description: Architect/writer; her Glass House is noted as possibly influenced by Rudofsky’s courtyard houses featured in the 'Brazil Builds' exposition (1940–1942).
shared_activities: conceptual influence via published exhibition precedent (Brazil Builds / courtyard houses)
connections.notes: Influence is stated as possible/attributed, not as a direct collaboration.

connections.relationship_description: Theatre director; collaborated with Bo Bardi on the 1959 exhibition 'Bahia in Ibirapuera' associated with the V São Paulo Bienal, combining objects, music, images, and craft from Bahia.
shared_activities: design and production of the 'Bahia' exhibition in Ibirapuera
biennial exhibition-making and cultural programming
connections.notes: The article identifies this as a crucial transitional moment in her exhibition design approach.

category_summaries.summary: Bo Bardi’s closest personal ties were to her parents (Enrico and Giovanna Bo), her sister Graziella, and especially her husband Pietro Maria Bardi, whose marriage was also a durable creative partnership shaping her Brazilian career.

Her professional network spans Italian wartime/postwar publishing and practice (Carlo Pagani, Gio Ponti, Bruno Zevi, Federico Patellani, Elio Vittorini) and Brazilian institution-building (Assis Chateaubriand, Giancarlo Palanti). Several additional ties are influence-based, where specific canonical architects informed key design decisions (e.g., MoMA’s 1939 building; Farnsworth House; Case Study House).

Bo Bardi’s artistic and curatorial relationships include direct collaboration with theatre director Martim Gonçalves and a set of explicitly cited avant-garde reference figures (El Lissitzky, Franco Albini) shaping her exhibition design language.

The provided Wikipedia text documents her role as a lecturer at the University of São Paulo and her efforts to secure a permanent position, but it does not name specific students, mentors, or departmental colleagues; therefore, academic ties are not expanded into person-to-person connections here.
